name: Chokha (Georgian Men's Coat)
description: The chokha is the traditional men's coat of the Caucasus, a long woollen garment with a fitted waist, a flared skirt and, most distinctively, rows of small cartridge cases - the gazyr - sewn diagonally across the chest. The gazyr began as real ammunition holders, with silver, wood or bone caps, and survived as ornament long after firearms made them obsolete, so the decorated chest became the emblem of Caucasian dress. In Georgia the chokha has been worn since at least the seventeenth century, with regional cuts: the Khevsur highland variant is richly embroidered in wool, while the plain dark chokha of the lowlands is the classic civic and military coat. After generations of everyday use the chokha is today reserved for festivals, folk dance, weddings and ceremonial occasions, and it remains the strongest single emblem of Georgian national dress.
source: Georgian National Museum, Tbilisi; ethnographic dress studies of the Caucasus

name: Kantsi (Georgian Drinking Horn)
description: The kantsi is the drinking horn of the Georgian highlands, cut from the curved horn of an ox, aurochs or mountain goat, polished, and often mounted at the rim in chased silver, sometimes with a small stand or a chain to hang it by. It is the fixed vessel of the supra, the Georgian feast, where the tamada raises the horn for each toast and custom requires it to be drained to the bottom in one draught before it is passed on; to drink from the kantsi is to honour the wine, the host and the speaker. The largest horns, holding a litre or more, are prized heirlooms of Svaneti and Khevsureti, and the same vessels appear in medieval Georgian manuscripts and in modern feast painting. Because the horn cannot be set down with wine in it, every toast must be finished, which is why the kantsi is remembered as the instrument of Georgian generosity.
material: ox or goat horn, chased silver (festive examples)
source: Russian Museum of Ethnography collections; Georgian feast (supra) custom studies

name: Panduri (Georgian Three-String Lute)
description: The panduri is the three-string fretted lute of eastern Georgia, a shallow wooden instrument carved from a single block of mulberry, walnut or other fruitwood, with a short neck, three strings and a soft, bright voice. It belongs to Kartli and Kakheti, where it accompanies men's table songs and the solo and choral polyphony of the region, the player strumming or plucking the strings to support the voice. Custom held that the panduri should hang on the wall of the house when not in use, ready for songs, and it was treated as a companion of family and village life rather than a mere concert instrument. With its larger four-string cousin the chonguri, the panduri is the most common plucked instrument of Georgian folk music and a familiar emblem of Georgian tradition, taught in music schools and played at every supra.
material: mulberry or other wood, gut/nylon strings
source: Georgian folk music tradition; hangebi.ge folk instrument documentation

name: Chonguri (Georgian Four-String Lute)
description: The chonguri is the four-string fretless lute of western Georgia, carved from a single block of walnut or maple into a shallow bowl, with a flat spruce soundboard and a short drone string called the zili that buzzes beneath the melody strings. It is the instrument of Guria and Samegrelo, where it traditionally accompanied women's songs and the nadi, the evening working gatherings at which women spun, wove and sang, and where the chonguri's quiet, flexible tone fitted a female voice. Unlike the fretted panduri of the east, the chonguri is played with a light, flowing touch, and its three melody strings are named after the three voices of Georgian polyphony. Still made and taught today, the chonguri belongs to the living polyphonic tradition that UNESCO inscribed in 2008.
material: walnut or maple, spruce soundboard, nylon strings
source: Smithsonian 'Georgian Chonguri' object of the day; Georgian folk instrument studies (Arakishvili)

name: Chuniri (Svan Bowed Fiddle)
description: The chuniri is the bowed fiddle of the Georgian mountain province of Svaneti, a round or tubular wooden body with a skin soundboard, three gut or horsehair strings and a heavy bow, held against the shoulder like a small violin. Because a bowed string can sustain a note, the chuniri is said to sing in place of a human voice, standing in for a singer in Svan hunting songs, work songs and choral polyphony; its two-string cousin, the chianuri, serves the same role in other highland regions such as Racha and Adjara. The instrument was the personal companion of Svan shepherds and hunters, who played it at home, at vigils and in the towers of the mountain villages. It remains one of the two bowed instruments of Georgia, heard at festivals and in the polyphonic ensembles that carry Svan tradition.
material: wood body, skin soundboard, horsehair strings
source: Wikipedia 'Chuniri'; Georgian folk music instrument documentation

name: Qvevri (Georgian Wine Vessel)
description: The qvevri is the great egg-shaped earthenware vessel of Georgia in which wine is fermented and aged, buried up to its neck in the floor of the marani, the wine cellar, so that only the clay rim and lid rise above the ground. Grape must, skins and stems all go into the qvevri and rest there for months, the cool earth holding a steady temperature, which gives amber wines their tannic, textured character and the method its special place in winemaking. Potters coil the vessels by hand from local clay, line them with beeswax and fire them without glaze; archaeological finds from the Shulaveri-Shomutepe culture date the method some 8,000 years, making qvevri wine among the oldest in the world. In 2013 UNESCO inscribed the ancient Georgian traditional qvevri wine-making method on the Representative List, and the buried qvevri remains the heart of Kakhetian cellar life.
source: UNESCO ICH 'Ancient Georgian traditional Qvevri wine-making method' (2013)

name: Khachkar (Armenian Cross-Stone)
description: The khachkar is the Armenian cross-stone, a freestanding stele carved from a single slab of local stone, most often the volcanic tuff of the Armenian plateau, its face dominated by an ornamented cross set over a rosette or a wheel of eternity. Around the cross the carver fills the stone with interlace, vine scrolls, leaves, pomegranates and birds, and the whole composition is framed in a decorated border; the earliest dated example bears the year 879, and the art reached its richest period from the thirteenth century. Khachkars were raised as tombstones, memorials for the dead, church dedications and thanksgivings, linking the everyday and the divine, the village and the monastery. In 2010 UNESCO inscribed the symbolism and craftsmanship of khachkars on the Representative List, and carved examples stand at Armenian churches from Julfa to Jerusalem.
material: volcanic tuff or other local stone
source: UNESCO ICH 'Armenian cross-stones art. Symbolism and craftsmanship of Khachkars' (2010)

name: Duduk (Armenian Double-Reed Flute)
description: The duduk is the double-reed woodwind of Armenia, carved from apricot wood into a short cylindrical tube fitted with a wide, flat reed, and played with circular breathing so the sound never stops. The technique of breathing in through the nose while squeezing air from the cheeks gives the duduk its characteristic long, breathy, singing notes, and the instrument is called the voice of Armenia for its warm, mournful tone. It accompanies folk songs, dances and round dances, but above all the lament, and it pairs with songs of mourning and love at weddings, funerals and the great feast days. In 2008 UNESCO inscribed duduk music on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and the instrument has also found a wider audience in world music and film scores.

name: Tar (Azerbaijani Long-Necked Lute)
description: The Azerbaijani tar is a long-necked plucked lute with a deep figure-of-eight body, a lambskin soundboard and three courses of steel strings, played with a small plectrum held between the fingers. Master-builders hollow the body from mulberry wood, and the instrument's design was refined in the nineteenth century, when the tar became the leading solo and ensemble instrument of Azerbaijani music. It leads the mugham trio of tar, kamancha and frame drum that performs the classical modal suites of Azerbaijani tradition, and it accompanies ashiq narrative song as well. In 2012 UNESCO inscribed the craftsmanship and performance art of the tar on the Representative List, and Azerbaijani composers have written concert works for the instrument, making it a rare folk lute with a classical repertoire.
material: mulberry wood, lambskin soundboard, steel strings
source: UNESCO ICH 'Craftsmanship and performance art of the Tar' (2012)

name: Kamancha (Azerbaijani Spike Fiddle)
description: The kamancha is the bowed spike fiddle of Azerbaijan, built with a spherical or bowl-shaped wooden body covered with fish- or lambskin, a long neck that pierces the body, and four steel strings, played upright with the bow resting on the knee. Its bright, precise tone carries well indoors, which is why the kamancha sits beside the tar in the mugham trio and in the ensembles of Azerbaijani folk music, doubling and answering the melodic line. The instrument has a long history across the Caucasus, Persia and Central Asia under the name kamancheh, and Azerbaijani craftsmen and players developed their own distinguished school. In 2017 UNESCO inscribed the art of crafting and playing the kamancha on the Representative List, and the instrument remains central both to classical mugham and to the folk music of weddings and festivals.
material: walnut or mulberry wood, skin soundboard, steel strings
source: UNESCO ICH 'Art of crafting and playing with kamancha' (2017)

name: Kelaghayi (Azerbaijani Silk Headscarf)
description: The kelaghayi is the square silk headscarf of Azerbaijani women, woven on narrow silk looms in the town of Sheki and the village of Basgal, then dyed and printed with woodblocks so that a patterned border frames a plainer field. The classic ornament is the buta, the curved teardrop or flame motif that runs along the edge, and the colours carry meaning: white and light shades for older women and mourning, red and bright colours for brides and young women. The scarf is folded and tied in many ways - under the chin, at the back, or draped over the shoulders - and it belongs to daily wear, weddings, funerals and religious observance alike, its symbolism bound up with the woman's age and occasion. In 2014 UNESCO inscribed the traditional art and symbolism of the kelaghayi on the Representative List, and silk masters in Basgal still print the scarves by hand.
era: silk tradition from c. 7th century; kelaghayi to present
source: UNESCO ICH 'Traditional art and symbolism of Kelaghayi' (2014)

name: Shebeke (Sheki Stained-Glass Lattice)
description: Shebeke is the stained-glass lattice window of the Azerbaijani town of Sheki, built by fitting hundreds of small panes of coloured glass into a web of walnut strips that hold together by interlocking notches, without glue, nails or any backing frame. Each joint is cut and fitted by hand, and a single panel can take months of patient work, which is why the masters call the craft the art of patience. The finest surviving example is the Sheki Khan's Palace of 1762, whose roughly 190 windows hold up to five thousand glass fragments, throwing soft blue, red and green light across the painted walls of the palace. Since the palace was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019, the surviving shebeke workshops have revived the craft, training new masters in the old joinery.
source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Historic Centre of Sheki with the Khan's Palace' (2019); Art of Shebeke (national ICH inventory)

name: Shahmaran Amulet
description: The Shahmaran amulet carries the image of the serpent queen of Caucasian and Anatolian legend, a being with the head of a beautiful woman and the body of a serpent, who is said to have taught healing and the secrets of nature to those who dwelt in her underground kingdom. Silver and brass amulets, pendants, bracelets and wall plaques bearing her figure are worn or hung to turn away the evil eye and to bring luck and health, and her serpent-woman form appears on carpets, on jewellery and throughout the traditional story cycle of Azerbaijan, Turkey and Iran. The British Museum holds amulets of the serpent queen, and the legend of Shahmaran survives strongly in folk belief, especially among women who seek her protection in childbirth and sickness. As a wearable image of a living folk deity, the Shahmaran amulet links ancient serpent worship to modern jewellery.
material: silver or brass, engraved or painted serpent-queen image
source: British Museum collection (E AF.77); Shahmaran legend of Azerbaijan and Anatolia

name: Lahij Copperware
description: Lahij copperware is the hammered copper and brass craft of the mountain village of Lahij in Azerbaijan's Ismayilli district, where smiths have worked for centuries in a tight warren of craftsmen's streets. A vessel such as an ewer, basin, cauldron or tray is raised from a single sheet of metal by hammering, never cast or soldered, then engraved with geometric rosettes, floral scrolls and inscriptions, and finally coated with a silvery tin alloy that protects the copper. The craft flourished in the nineteenth century, when Lahij's copper goods travelled the Silk Road and were sold in Baku, Tbilisi and Persian cities, and the village's self-governing craft guilds kept the techniques alive. In 2015 UNESCO inscribed the copper craftsmanship of Lahij on the Representative List, and master coppersmiths still work in the old street, training apprentices in hammer, chisel and furnace.

name: Azerbaijani Carpet
description: The Azerbaijani carpet is the hand-knotted pile rug of Azerbaijan, woven on vertical looms in distinct regional schools - Karabakh, Shirvan, Tabriz, Baku, Gazakh and Ganja among them - each with its own palette, knot and field layout. The traditional repertoire of motifs includes the buta, the dragon, the medallion, the stylised garden and the khoncha offering tray, and the carpets combine rich reds, blues and ivories dyed from madder, indigo and walnut husk. Weaving was and is a women's craft, learned in the family, with the design passing from mother to daughter and the loom set up for dowry carpets that would serve the household for generations. In 2010 UNESCO inscribed the traditional art of Azerbaijani carpet weaving on the Representative List, and the carpet remains Azerbaijan's best-known craft, displayed in national museums and in the carpet museum of Baku.
material: wool pile, cotton warp, natural dyes
era: attested from the Middle Ages; classical schools 16th-19th century
source: UNESCO ICH 'Traditional art of Azerbaijani carpet weaving' (2010)
